title: How to Build a Legacy Technology Risk Management Plan Under the Australian Government’s Protective Security Policy Framework
summary: Learn how to build a technology risk management plan for PSPF Direction 002-2026 with practical steps for legacy technology stocktakes & risk mitigation.
body_markdown:
[PSPF Direction 002-2026](https://www.protectivesecurity.gov.au/publications-library/direction-002-2026-strengthening-commonwealth-cyber-posture-against-ai-enabled-risks) requires non-corporate Commonwealth entities to complete a Legacy Technology Stocktake, develop a Legacy Technology Risk Management Plan and report both to Home Affairs by 31 March 2027. Entities operating Systems of Government Significance (SoGS) face an earlier deadline of 31 December 2026.


This blog focuses on execution: how to build the inventory, decide what should retire or retain and attach evidence to the controls that protect unsupported software.


## How do you conduct a Legacy Technology Stocktake?


Below is a six-step process to run the stocktake, with scope and evidence standards agreed before collection begins.


1. Set the scope and contact contractors on day one. Include systems managed by or on behalf of the entity, and ask providers to return inventories in the same structure as the internal register.
2. Start from existing records. Use the CMDB, asset register and 2024 technology asset stocktake rather than beginning with a blank sheet.
3. Record vendor support status. Capture the exact product, version, patch level and whether it is supported, on extended support, out of support or end-of-life. Use vendor lifecycle sources for Oracle, SAP, VMware and Microsoft. For open-source components, record project maintenance status. For bespoke systems, record who can still change the code.
4. Map dependencies. Record integrations, downstream services and the operational consequence if the system becomes unavailable.
5. Prioritise public-facing and SoGS systems. The direction prioritises public-facing services, while Systems of Government Significance carry an earlier deadline.
6. Name an owner for every system. Record both the business owner and technical owner so every line has someone responsible for need, change and evidence.


### What should your legacy technology register capture?


A workable register uses one row per system. These core fields are the starting point for the stocktake. Find additional details in our eBook, “[A Guide to Enterprise Software Security and Modernisation for Australian Government Agencies](https://www.riministreet.com/info/enterprise-software-security-australian-government-agencies/) ”.


Field Definition


System name Name used by the business


Business owner Who depends on it and signs the statement of need


Technical owner Who can change it


Vendor support status Supported, extended support, out of support or end-of-life, with date


Public-facing Yes or no


SoGS Yes or no


Category A Meets one or more: considered an end-of-life product, or out of support and extended support from the manufacturer, vendor or developer


Category B Meets one or more: impractical to update or support within the entity, no longer cost-effective, considered to be above the current acceptable risk threshold, offers diminishing business utility, or prevents or obstructs fulfilment of the entity’s IT strategies


Legacy Yes


if it meets one or more criteria in both Category A and Category B


Decision Retire, remediate or migrate, or retain with controls


Review date When the decision is next checked


The decision and review date fields turn the inventory into an auditable plan because they tie each system to an owner, a treatment and a point of re-assessment.


## What goes in a Legacy Technology Risk Management Plan?


The direction names four parts the plan must have. Home Affairs has not published a template or required format, so these four parts are the working risk management plan template, and the Commonwealth Security Policy Branch is the place to ask what it expects to see.


1. A target to reduce legacy systems. Set the target in line with the entity’s risk tolerance and appetite and apply it to systems that meet both Category A and Category B.
2. Prioritisation strategies. Explain which systems will be treated first, beginning with public-facing and SoGS systems and then ranking by consequence.
3. Mitigations for systems that remain. Record the controls, evidence and person who approved the residual risk.
4. Procedures to rationalise the technology estate. Explain how the entity will continue finding, reviewing and retiring systems after the initial deadline.


For each system, document one decision path:


- If it is no longer needed, retire it after records and dependency checks.
- If it does not meet risk requirements, treat the gaps and reassess. Migrate if residual risk remains unacceptable.
- If it can be supported and protected in place, retain it with approved controls and a review date.
- If retaining it creates verified savings, record the financial evidence. Do not assume reinvestment funding that has not been validated.


A plan built this way allows an auditor to follow the reason, evidence, owner and approval for every retained or retired system.


## Can unsupported software stay in service under the PSPF?


Yes, unsupported software can continue to stay in operation where continued operation is justified, risks are appropriately mitigated and all other applicable requirements are met under PSPF Direction 002-2026. The direction does not ask for every unsupported system to be replaced. It asks for “mitigations to address risks arising from continued sustainment of legacy technology systems”, which recognises that some systems will stay. The entity should document the risk, apply compensating controls and demonstrate that critical vulnerabilities can still be patched or shielded.


For each retained unsupported system, controls may include:


- Keep fixes coming. Maintain a support arrangement that provides security fixes, tax and regulatory updates and break-fix services after vendor support ends. Third-party support is a proven option for SAP ECC, Oracle E-Business Suite, Oracle Database or VMware environments, as well as many other systems. Evidence: contract and fix history.
- Isolate it. Segment the network so the system is reachable only from required locations. Evidence: network diagram and firewall rules.
- Shield it. Use virtual patching at the network or application layer where appropriate. Evidence: the rule for each critical CVE and the test demonstrating it works.
- Watch it. Tune logging and monitoring to the system. Evidence: log sources and alert rules.
- Restrict access. Reduce accounts, strengthen authentication and remove standing administrative access. Evidence: access review.
- Document and approve it. Record residual risk, controls, owner and review date, with acceptance by an authorised person. Evidence: signed risk acceptance.


The key test is whether each control can be evidenced against the actual vulnerabilities and risks affecting the system. A system that cannot be patched or shielded, or has no valid business reason to remain, belongs on the retirement or migration path.


## What should an entity do first?


Pull the 2024 technology asset stocktake as a starting point, then expand it to cover all systems managed by, or on behalf of, the entity, and add a vendor support end date to every line. Then apply the Category A and Category B tests, beginning with public-facing and SoGS systems.


Use the register to assign decisions, controls, evidence, acceptance authorities and review dates. This creates the working core of the Legacy Technology Risk Management Plan.

## Conclusion


The stocktake is complete only when each in-scope system has a support status, owner, dependency view, PSPF classification and documented decision. The plan then turns those decisions into reduction targets, prioritisation, controls and ongoing estate rationalisation.


### Key Takeaways


A robust stocktake begins with a consistent register covering internal and contractor-managed systems. The risk plan must set a reduction target, prioritise systems, document mitigations and establish ongoing rationalisation. Unsupported software may remain where risk is accepted and controls are evidenced.
